FunkyMushroom · Nov 20, 2026

The related economic concept here is the Broken Window Fallacy. Doing 'redundant' work doesn't improve the economy, because there's an opportunity cost doing to anything. And replacing the need to "fix broken windows" or do now-AI-automated work would free up that opportunity cost. Which is how it's worked for nearly all automation. (Though Computers are subject to long running debate about this. See the Solow Productivity Paradox)

The gigawatt-sized asterisk on all of this is that AI companies have to capture that $1 billion. Anthropic has to ten-fold increase it's revenues or it goes bankrupt under it's current commitments. It has to increase it's revenues another 10 times to reach the $10,000,000,000,000/yr revenue required to support it's current valuation.

Anthropic put their Total Addressable Market at 35% of Global GDP (~$40 trillion/yr). They're planning to capture all of the money.

The second gigawatt-sized asterisk is that because of the fine handiwork of Mr. Huang, China has made very competitive AI models available for free, so the actual ability for AI companies to capture the value of the labour they displace ends up being quite limited. Thus a problem in the predictions: Something as to break, but it is as of yet unclear what that will be. Maybe Chinese AI will be banned, maybe Anthropic & OpenAI go bankrupt.

throw0101c · Nov 20, 2026

> I am trying to understand something about the economy and AI. If AI disrupts an industry that previously had high wages and now can be automated by commodity AI products, would it not actually lower GDP in some way (initially anyway)?

Pre-AI, if you spent $X you got A units of output; post-AI:

* if you need 'only' A units, you will spend less than $X (technically lower GDP)

* but if the limiting factor was not the desired units, but your budget, you will continue to spend $X but get >A units (same GDP)

Additionally, if each unit is less expensive, this allows the end-customers to spend less on it, and reallocate some of their budget to other things, which would keep the overall GDP the same.

LarsDu88 · Nov 21, 2026

Over the long term the economy will grow. That I am 100% confident of. When you take previously scarce resources and commoditize them, the knock on effects tend to spread widely. Intelligence and automation used to be enormously expensive, and now they are becoming cheaper by the day. Right now, frontier LLMs, which I consider wildly inefficient can give you mostly functional blueprints and diagrams for working products, like basic electronics on top of the image generation and code generation that is increasingly being commoditized.

The goods and services built atop "tech" should start to become cheaper as well. For knowledge workers this is terrible, but for consumers, this is great. I think folks worrying about an economic collapse are only looking at this from the perspective of knowledge workers and not from the much larger population of consumers.

The effect on the AI companies with pure competition is to make them basically worthless unless they find ways of stifling competition. For example by banning open weight AI in the name of safety, forming a global monopoly, buying up all the RAM capacity in the world, etc. All of this stuff is going on right now.

The value is there. The true question is whether the wealth will be concentrated and captured or released and distributed. I'm in the camp the likely outcome is actually the former. The destruction you're imagining is the "loss" of the ~$1B in transactions that consumers were previously paying to employ $1B worth of jobs. Consumers actually just have that extra $1B to spend, and people previously making about $1B now have about $1B worth of labor to direct elsewhere.

Economies don't really lose jobs. Buyers lose demand for products, and employers lose demand for particular kinds of labor. That doesn't make the labor less valuable to anybody else, it just means their current employer couldn't afford it or use it. The same number of people with the same set of skills still want to work as before.

It's actually common for labor to increase in value even when it gets disrupted! What happens is a rebalancing of the labor market away from obsoleted industries/company/products nobody wants, towards those that leverage the disruptive technology. Consider dotcom: eventually some of those employees left tech, and the rest created the actually-valuable Internet businesses because they regrouped and started different things.

Otherwise when there isn't enough demand for employable people to find work, central banks lend (or print) more money until employers want to hire them, because they're leaving money on the table from consumers' unmet demand if they don't.

In short: economies don't produce jobs. Jobs are what happen when demand on the labor market meets supply; creating more aggregate demand is easy but even then, it creates demand for labor to provide what people want to pay for.

GDP growth is usually measured in “volume”, which means that the demand for a good or service doubles while the price is divided by ten, the GDP share for this good or service doubles even if the amount of money is 5 times less.

The reverse is also true though, which means if something becomes twice as expensive (say oil) and people starts buying less of it, it's share of GDP will diminish. Because of that, the GDP deflator is underestimating inflation, and overestimating actual growth in times of high inflation.
